According to the guidelines for national tuberculosis (TB) programs, a TB patient with an unknown HIV status is defined as any individual with bacteriologically confirmed or clinically diagnosed TB who has no documented HIV test results and no evidence of enrollment in HIV care. If the HIV status is later determined, the patient should be reclassified accordingly. 2. TB cases are classified based on drug resistance patterns determined through drug susceptibility testing (DST) of clinical isolates confirmed to be Mycobacterium tuberculosis. The classifications are as follows: Monoresistance: Resistance to only one first-line anti-TB drug. Polyresistance: Resistance to more than one first-line anti-TB drug, excluding both isoniazid and rifampicin. Multidrug resistance (MDR): Resistance to at least both isoniazid and rifampicin. Extensive drug resistance (XDR): Resistance to any fluoroquinolone and at least one of the three second-line injectable drugs (capreomycin, kanamycin, or amikacin), in addition to MDR. Rifampicin resistance (RR): Resistance to rifampicin detected through phenotypic or genotypic methods, with or without resistance to other anti-TB drugs. This includes monoresistance, MDR, polyresistance, or XDR. 3. These drug resistance categories are not mutually exclusive. For example, rifampicin-resistant TB (RR-TB) includes cases of MDR-TB and XDR-TB. While monoresistance and polyresistance have traditionally been limited to first-line drugs, future drug regimens may necessitate classification based on resistance patterns to fluoroquinolones, second-line injectable agents, and other anti-TB drugs as reliable DST becomes available. 4. Treatment outcomes for TB patients are defined consistently for both children and adults. For children with smear-negative pulmonary TB (PTB), smear-not-done PTB, or extrapulmonary TB (EPTB), treatment response is assessed monthly by monitoring weight gain and symptom improvement. For children with smear-positive TB, sputum smears should be repeated at 2 and 5 months. 5. The new treatment outcome definitions distinguish between two groups of patients: Those treated for drug-susceptible TB. Those treated for drug-resistant TB using second-line regimens (combination chemotherapy including drugs beyond Group 1). 6. Patients with drug-resistant TB who are started on second-line treatment are removed from the drug-susceptible TB outcome cohort. Coordination between the standard TB register and the second-line TB treatment register is essential to ensure accurate accounting of treatment outcomes. 7. Patients with RR-TB or MDR-TB strains should be promptly started on an appropriate second-line drug regimen. 8. Treatment outcomes for TB patients (excluding those treated for RR-TB or MDR-TB) are defined as follows: Cured: A pulmonary TB patient with bacteriologically confirmed TB at the start of treatment who is smearor culture-negative in the last month of treatment and on at least one previous occasion. Treatment completed: A TB patient who completed treatment without evidence of failure but without documented negative smear or culture results in the last month of treatment and on at least one previous occasion. Treatment failed: A TB patient whose sputum smear or culture remains positive at month 5 or later during treatment. Died: A TB patient who dies for any reason before or during treatment. Lost to follow-up: A TB patient who did not start treatment or whose treatment was interrupted for 2 consecutive months or more. Not evaluated: A TB patient for whom no treatment outcome is assigned, including cases transferred out to another treatment unit or cases with unknown outcomes. 9. For RR-TB/MDR-TB/XDR-TB patients treated with second-line regimens, treatment outcomes are defined as: Cured: Treatment completed as per national policy, with no evidence of failure and at least three consecutive negative cultures taken at least 30 days apart after the intensive phase. Treatment completed: Treatment completed as per national policy without evidence of failure, but without documentation of three consecutive negative cultures. Treatment failed: Treatment terminated or a permanent regimen change involving at least two anti-TB drugs due to lack of conversion by the end of the intensive phase, bacteriological reversion in the continuation phase, additional acquired resistance to fluoroquinolones or second-line injectables, or adverse drug reactions. Died: A patient who dies for any reason during treatment. Lost to follow-up: A patient whose treatment was interrupted for 2 consecutive months or more. Not evaluated: A patient for whom no treatment outcome is assigned, including cases transferred out to another unit with unknown outcomes. 10. Conversion to negative culture is defined as two consecutive negative cultures taken at least 30 days apart. Reversion to positive culture is defined as two consecutive positive cultures after an initial conversion, occurring during the continuation phase. 11. Tuberculin skin testing (TST) involves the intradermal injection of mycobacterial antigens to elicit a delayed-type hypersensitivity response, measured as induration in millimeters. The Mantoux method is the standard for identifying Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection. Multiple puncture tests are unreliable and should not be used. 12. TST results should be read 48–72 hours after administration. Induration of ≥5 mm is considered positive in HIV-positive children and severely malnourished children. Induration of ≥10 mm is positive in all other children, regardless of BCG vaccination status. 13. Gastric aspiration is a technique used to collect gastric contents for microscopy and mycobacterial culture in young children who cannot produce sputum. It is most useful in hospitalized children and should be performed in the early morning after fasting. The diagnostic yield of three gastric aspirates is approximately 25–50%, and a negative result does not exclude TB. 14. Gastric aspiration should be performed as an inpatient procedure at the child’s bedside or in a procedure room. The child must fast for at least 4 hours (3 hours for infants) before the procedure.
